newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weak yen expected to rev up profits at Nissan.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen expected to rev up profits at Nissan.

text.p: Japan's second biggest carmaker, Nissan Motor Co Ltd, is expected to have raced to sharply higher profits for the year which ended in March and should continue to reap the benefits of the weaker yen.

Analysts say Nissan is likely to have seen its parent current profits more than double in the 1996/97 business year and should maintain upward momentum through the current year -- although profits may rise at a less dramatic pace.
On a group net basis, analysts expect the carmaker to post its first annual profit in five years for 1996/97.

Despite the dollar's slip in the past week, the average exchange rate for the current year is still likely to benefit big exporters like Nissan, helping to boost overseas sales and keep profits on a rising curve, the analysts said.
Nissan will announce its actual profits for 1996/97 and its forecast for the current business year at the end of May.

Analysts attributed the expected surge in profits to a weaker yen trend relative to the previous year, which has given Japanese automakers a competitive edge overseas and sounded alarm bells at rival car companies, particularly in the United States. They also said cost-cutting was a factor.

They expect the 1996/97 parent current profits to range between 84 billion yen ($705 million) and 90 billion yen ($756 million) compared with an actual 32.43 billion yen ($272 million) a year earlier. In November, Nissan revised up its forecast for 1996/97 parent current profit to 80 billion yen ($672 million) from a May forecast of 70 billion yen ($588 million), due to an expected windfall from a weaker yen.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on non-operating activities such as stock investments.
On a group net basis, the analysts' forecasts for 1996/97 ranged from a profit of 55 billion yen ($462 million) to a profit of 60 billion yen ($504 million).
Analysts also made projections for the firm's profits in the current year, which started in April, on the assumption that the dollar's recent slip would be a temporary phenomenon.
They said the average dollar exchange rate for the year to end-March 1998 would likely be 120 yen, compared with an actual average of 113.34 yen in 1996/97 and 96.80 yen the year before.
On Monday, the dollar dipped below 118 yen to a nearly four-month low, but recovered to around 119.35 yen on Tuesday.

"Nissan's parent current profit is likely to be 97 billion yen ($815 million) in 1997/98 on the assumption that the average dollar/yen rate will be 120 yen," said Kankaku Research senior analyst Nobuaki Yanachi.
He said that a dollar rise by one yen translates into eight billion yen ($67.2 million) of annual profit for Nissan, by making its products more competitive in overseas markets.
Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura saw Nissan's 1997/98 current profit even higher, at 105 billion yen ($882 million).

Yanachi said Nissan's 1996/97 profits were held back by appraisal losses on shares held in other firms, such as Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd. His forecast for 1996/97 was for parent current profit of 84 billion yen ($705 million).
Nissan's business had been hit hard in the past few years by the strong yen and after-effects of the collapse of Japan's late-1980s bubble economy.

But the company's business is finally showing signs of picking up. Domestic sales volume rose 0.5 percent to 1.13 million units in 1996/97, and exports rose 0.8 percent to 598,244, according to Nissan data.
Nissan officials have said the firm should post a group net profit in 1996/97, the first in five years. They gave no specific estimates.

A Nissan spokeswoman said the firm expects to stay in the black in 1997/98 due to rising local sales and exports at its Mexican unit, as well as higher sales in Europe. In 1995/96, Nissan made a group net loss of 88.42 billion yen ($743 million) due to losses at overseas units.

Sugiura estimated Nissan's group net profit would be 65 billion yen ($546 million) in 1997/98, while Yanachi's forecast was for a profit of 70 billion yen ($588 million) to 80 billion yen ($672 million), depending on exchange rate levels. ($1=119 yen)
